Before the pilot, record a comparable baseline across representative weeks, accounting for seasonality, holidays, and promotions. Track customer access (visits, enquiries, wait times, and missed or redirected requests), sales and gross margin by time period, and total staffing cost—including all employee and subcontractor hours, overtime, and any added opening or closing work. Compare results with the baseline, using consistent measures; show legal-minimum pay costs separately from a credible living-wage target. Review customer feedback and staff impacts, then extend the trial or adopt the change only if the pilot supports it.

To pilot new opening hours effectively, a business should first establish a baseline by tracking key metrics during representative weeks before the pilot. These metrics should include customer access indicators such as the number of visits, inquiries made, wait times experienced by customers, and instances of missed or redirected requests. The business should also monitor sales and gross margin by time period to understand the revenue impact of the new hours. Additionally, it should track total staffing costs, encompassing all employee and subcontractor hours worked, overtime incurred, and any additional costs associated with opening or closing during the new hours.

During the pilot, the business should continue to track these same metrics to compare the outcomes with the baseline data. This comparison should be done using consistent measures to ensure accuracy. It's also advisable to differentiate between legal-minimum pay costs and costs associated with a credible living-wage target for staff. Furthermore, the business should review customer feedback and assess any impacts on staff, including their experiences and any challenges faced during the pilot hours.

The decision to extend the trial or adopt the new opening hours permanently should be based on whether the pilot's results support the change. If the data indicates improved customer access, sales, or operational efficiency without negatively impacting staff or significantly increasing costs, the business may consider adopting the new hours. Conversely, if the pilot reveals significant drawbacks, such as decreased customer satisfaction, reduced sales, or increased staffing costs without corresponding benefits, the business may need to adjust its plans or revert to the original hours.
